common_name: Blue Shield Louisiana Iris (Velvety Dark Navy Blue Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Claude Davis introduced Blue Shield as a seedling of 'New Offering', bearing a velvety dark navy blue self set off by a yellow-orange signal on well-branched stalks blooming midseason. It became an important breeding parent, standing behind later dark-toned Louisiana iris cultivars. Grow it in full sun with consistently moist to wet soil, and divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom to keep the deep color saturated.

common_name: New Offering Louisiana Iris (Dark Blue-Violet DeBaillon Award Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Claude Davis bred New Offering from 'Flat Top' crossed with the species Iris giganticaerulea, producing dark blue-violet flowers heavily veined in prunella violet with chartreuse haft markings on tall, well-branched stalks blooming midseason to late. It earned the Mary Swords DeBaillon Award and went on to parent influential later cultivars including 'Blue Shield'. Grow it in full sun with steady moisture, and divide congested clumps every four to five years in late summer to sustain vigorous bloom.

common_name: Atchafalaya Louisiana Iris (Velvety Dark Red-Violet Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Farron Campbell bred Atchafalaya from 'John's Lucifer' x 'Jeri', producing velvety, very dark red-violet flowers with a fine silver halo, yellow signals, and green crests on all petals, opening in a lightly ruffled, cartwheel-shaped form early in the midseason window. It earned an Award of Merit and has since been used as a breeding parent for later cultivars. Grow it in full sun with consistently moist to wet soil, and divide congested clumps every four to five years in late summer to maintain vigor.

common_name: Easter Tide Louisiana Iris (Lavender-Blue and Yellow DeBaillon Medal Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Charles W. Arny bred Easter Tide from 'Lucile Holley' crossed with a lavender seedling, producing lavender-blue standards over light yellow falls marked with an irregular deep orange-yellow signal and broad lavender-pink style arms, blooming on well-branched stalks in midseason. It earned the Society for Louisiana Irises' DeBaillon Award and later the DeBaillon Medal, and was used by later hybridizers as a breeding parent. Grow it in full sun with consistently wet soil, and divide congested clumps every four to five years in late summer to keep flowering strong.

common_name: German Coast Louisiana Iris (Purple-Violet Crepe-Textured Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: New Orleans hybridizer Patrick O'Connor bred German Coast from 'Faubourg St. John' crossed onto itself, producing purple standards streaked violet-purple at the midrib over crepe-textured purple-violet falls with a yellow arrowhead signal, on well-branched stalks blooming midseason. O'Connor later used it as a parent for a DeBaillon Medal-winning cultivar. Grow it in full sun with rich, constantly moist soil, and divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom to maintain vigor.

common_name: Henry Rowlan Louisiana Iris (Blue-Purple Gold-Signal Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: M. D. Faith bred Henry Rowlan from a 'Voodoo Song' cross, producing blue-purple standards and style arms over slightly deeper blue-purple falls marked with a bold golden-yellow signal, carried on vigorous, well-foliaged stalks blooming in early midseason. Patrick O'Connor later used it as a parent for a Mary Swords DeBaillon Medal-winning cultivar. Grow it in full sun with consistently moist to wet soil, and divide congested clumps every four to five years in late summer to sustain strong bloom.

common_name: Bout Midnight Louisiana Iris (Deep Velvety Black-Purple Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Mary Dunn bred Bout Midnight from a line tracing through 'Queen O' Queens' and 'Mrs. Ira Nelson' crossed with 'Dark Tide', producing very dark purple standards over falls of the same color overlaid with deep velvety black and a tiny gold line signal. It was later used by a subsequent hybridizer, crossed with 'Margaret Lee', to produce a DeBaillon Medal-winning cultivar. Grow it in full sun with consistently wet soil, and divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom to keep the dark color saturated.

common_name: Margaret Lee Louisiana Iris (Ruffled Magenta-Pink Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: John C. Taylor bred Margaret Lee from 'Dazzling Star' x 'Helen Naish', producing heavily ruffled magenta-pink standards with a green-influenced buff reverse over deeper magenta-pink falls carrying a large yellow signal, blooming midseason to late. It was later used as a parent, crossed with 'Bout Midnight', to produce a DeBaillon Medal-winning cultivar. Grow it in full sun with consistently moist to wet soil, and divide congested clumps every four to five years in late summer to maintain vigor.

common_name: Distance Bearded Iris (Historic 1946 Silvery Light Blue Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost; Distance is a historically significant mid-20th-century tall bearded iris and an ancestor of later dark blue bearded iris cultivars.

directions: Hybridized by Paul Cook from a cross of 'Castalia' x 'Santa Barbara' and 'Great Lakes', Distance bears silvery light blue, flaring, ruffled and waved flowers with a cool, translucent quality that period catalogs likened to the blue of a winter twilight. It won an Award of Merit and became an important parent behind later Dykes Medal-winning dark blue bearded iris. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom, and keep rhizomes in full sun with sharp drainage to avoid rot.
